title: The intermediate value theorem proved
objectives: Prove the intermediate value theorem from completeness.

screens.title: Halve and keep the sign change
screens.prose: $f(x) = x^3 - x - 1$ has $f(1) = -1 < 0$ and $f(2) = 5 > 0$. Halve $[1, 2]$ at its midpoint $m$. Keep the half whose ends have opposite signs, and repeat. The table gives $f$ at each midpoint.

state.caption: Each midpoint you type appears as a dot.

screens.question: Type the five midpoints in order.

hints.text: Step 1 halves $[1, 2]$, so $m = 1.5$. There $f > 0$, while $f(1) < 0$.
So keep $[1, 1.5]$; step 2 uses $m = 1.25$, where $f < 0$. Keep $[1.25, 1.5]$.

byKey.r1c1: Check step 2. $f(1.5) > 0$ and $f(1) < 0$, so the sign change is in $[1, 1.5]$: halve that.

explain.text: Each step keeps a half with a sign change, so the intervals are nested. After step 5 the root lies in $[1.3125, 1.34375]$. After 10 steps it lies in $[1.32421875, 1.3251953125]$, around 1.324718.

screens.prose: Keep going. After 10 halvings the interval is $[1.32421875, 1.3251953125]$, drawn below. The dot is the root, about 1.324718.
screens.question: How wide is the interval after 10 halvings?

hints.text: The first interval has width 1.
Each step halves the width.
After 10 steps the width is $\tfrac{1}{2^{10}}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Halve the width 1 ten times.

explain.text: The width after $n$ steps is $\tfrac{1}{2^n}$, so after 10 it is $\tfrac{1}{1024} \approx 0.000977$. The nested intervals close in on one point. Completeness, through nested intervals, says that point exists.

screens.title: The intermediate value theorem
screens.prose: **Intermediate value theorem.** If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and $f(a) < 0 < f(b)$, then $f(c) = 0$ for some $c$ in $(a, b)$. Applied to $f - y$, it says $f$ takes every value $y$ between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$.
screens.question: What does the theorem promise for $x^3 - x - 1$ on $[1, 2]$?

options.why: You added uniqueness. The theorem promises at least one root; uniqueness here needs another argument, such as $f$ increasing.
You placed the root. The theorem says a root exists, not where; $f(1.5) = 0.875$.

options.text: A rational root, found after finitely many halvings.
options.why: You expected bisection to stop. The root 1.3247... is irrational; bisection only closes in on it.

hints.text: Read the conclusion of the theorem word for word.
It says 'for some $c$'.
Some means at least one.

feedback.correct: Right. At least one root, somewhere inside.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Separate what the theorem says from what bisection computes.

explain.text: The theorem gives existence: at least one root in $(1, 2)$. It does not say where, or how many. Bisection then locates a root to any accuracy.

screens.title: Where the negative part ends
screens.prose: Now a proof from completeness. Let $S = \{x \in [a, b] : f(x) < 0\}$ and $c = \sup S$. The segment on the axis is $S$ for our cubic, and its right end is the root.
screens.question: Why does $c = \sup S$ exist?

options.text: $S$ is non-empty, since $a \in S$, and bounded above by $b$. Completeness gives a supremum.
$S$ has a largest element, which is $c$.
options.why: You assumed a maximum. Here $S = [1, c)$ has none; completeness supplies a supremum instead.
You used continuity too early. A sup exists for any non-empty set bounded above; continuity comes in later.
You guessed a point. The sup is where the negative part ends, here near 1.3247, not 1.5.

hints.text: Completeness needs two things of a set.
Is $S$ non-empty? Is it bounded above?
$f(a) < 0$ puts $a$ in $S$, and every point of $S$ is at most $b$.

feedback.correct: Right. Non-empty and bounded above, so $\sup S$ exists.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the two hypotheses of the completeness axiom from l3.

explain.text: $a \in S$ and $S \subseteq [a, b]$, so completeness gives $c = \sup S$ with $a \le c \le b$. We do not yet know $f(c)$. The next two steps rule out $f(c) < 0$ and $f(c) > 0$.

screens.title: Case 1: $f(c) < 0$
screens.prose: Suppose $f(c) < 0$, as at the dot. Then $c < b$, and continuity at $c$ gives $\delta > 0$ with $f < 0$ on $(c - \delta, c + \delta) \cap [a, b]$. So some $x > c$ is in $S$.

state.caption: A pretend $c$ with $f(c) < 0$. Points just right of it are in $S$ too.

screens.question: Which property of $c$ does that contradict?

options.text: $c$ is an upper bound of $S$: no point of $S$ lies above $c$.
$c$ is the least upper bound: no smaller number bounds $S$.
options.why: You picked the other half of the sup. A point of $S$ above $c$ breaks being an upper bound at all.
You checked the wrong set fact. $S$ still holds $a$; the trouble is a point of $S$ above $c$.
You blamed the tool. Continuity is what found the point above $c$.

hints.text: The new point $x$ is in $S$ and $x > c$.
What does it mean for $c$ to be an upper bound of $S$?
Every point of $S$ is at most $c$; this $x$ is not.

feedback.correct: Right. A point of $S$ above $c$ means $c$ is not an upper bound.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the new point with $c$, and recall what an upper bound promises.

explain.text: Take $x = \min(c + \tfrac{\delta}{2}, b)$. Then $x > c$, $x \in [a, b]$ and $f(x) < 0$, so $x \in S$. That contradicts $c$ being an upper bound, so $f(c) \ge 0$.

screens.title: Case 2: $f(c) > 0$
screens.prose: Suppose $f(c) > 0$. Then $c > a$, and continuity gives $\delta > 0$ with $f > 0$ on $(c - \delta, c]$. So no point of $S$ lies in $(c - \delta, c]$.

state.caption: A pretend $c$ with $f(c) > 0$. Nothing just left of it is in $S$.

screens.question: Which property of $c$ does that contradict?

options.text: $c$ is the least upper bound: $c - \delta$ is a smaller upper bound.

options.why: You picked the wrong half. $c$ is still above every point of $S$; what fails is that nothing smaller bounds $S$.
You assumed $c \in S$. A sup need not belong to the set, and here $f(c) > 0$ says it does not.
You checked the end. $c \le b$ still holds; the trouble is a smaller upper bound.

hints.text: Every point of $S$ is at most $c$, and none lies in $(c - \delta, c]$.
So every point of $S$ is at most $c - \delta$.
Then $c - \delta$ is an upper bound smaller than $c$.

feedback.correct: Right. $c - \delta$ is an upper bound below $c$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find an upper bound of $S$ that is smaller than $c$.

explain.text: Points of $S$ are at most $c$, and none lies in $(c - \delta, c]$. So all are at most $c - \delta$, an upper bound below the least one. Hence $f(c) \le 0$, and with case 1, $f(c) = 0$.

screens.title: The whole proof
screens.prose: Assemble the proof of the theorem for continuous $f$ on $[a, b]$ with $f(a) < 0 < f(b)$. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: Let $S = \{x \in [a, b] : f(x) < 0\}$. It holds $a$ and is bounded by $b$, so $c = \sup S$ exists.
If $f(c) < 0$, continuity gives a point of $S$ above $c$. That contradicts $c$ being an upper bound.
If $f(c) > 0$, continuity gives $f > 0$ on $(c - \delta, c]$. Then $c - \delta$ is a smaller upper bound, a contradiction.
So $f(c) = 0$, and $c \ne a, b$ because $f(a) < 0 < f(b)$. $\blacksquare$
Every $x \in S$ has $f(x) < 0$, and $c$ is a limit of points of $S$, so $f(c) < 0$.
lines.why: You passed a strict inequality to a limit. Limits keep $\le$, not $<$: here $f(c) = 0$.

hints.text: Define the set and its sup first.
Then rule out each wrong sign; the two cases are independent.
Order: set and sup, the two cases (either order), conclusion.

feedback.correct: Right. A sup, two impossible signs, so $f(c) = 0$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Build $c = \sup S$, rule out $f(c) < 0$ and $f(c) > 0$, then conclude.

byKey.d1: You kept $<$ in the limit. $f(c) = \lim f(x_n) \le 0$ only, which is why case 2 is still needed.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: Completeness gives $c$; continuity rules out each strict sign. Both hypotheses are used, so neither can be dropped. The two cases may come in either order.

screens.title: A second proof, by halving
screens.prose: Bisection is a proof too. Keep halves with $f(a_n) < 0 \le f(b_n)$, starting from $[a_0, b_0] = [a, b]$. One line is flawed.
screens.question: Put the proof in order. Move the flawed line to Left out.

lines.text: The intervals $[a_n, b_n]$ are nested, with $b_n - a_n = \tfrac{b - a}{2^n}$.
By the nested interval property (l3), some $c$ lies in every $[a_n, b_n]$, and $a_n \to c$, $b_n \to c$.
By the sequential criterion (l15), $f(a_n) \to f(c)$ and $f(b_n) \to f(c)$.
Since $b_n - a_n \to 0$, some interval has length 0, and its one point is the root.
lines.why: No interval in the list has length 0. The root comes from nested intervals, not from a last step.

hints.text: Start with what halving does to the lengths.
Then find $c$ from completeness, and use continuity along $a_n$ and $b_n$.
Order: lengths, nested intervals give $c$, continuity, signs.

feedback.correct: Right. Nested intervals give $c$; continuity carries the signs to it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Get $c$ from the nested intervals first, then pass $f$ to the limit.

byKey.d1: You stopped the halving. Every interval has positive length; the point $c$ comes from completeness.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs. Only the flawed line goes to Left out.

explain.text: The halving builds nested intervals whose lengths tend to 0. Completeness, as nested intervals, gives $c$; continuity gives $f(c) \le 0 \le f(c)$. The same steps are the algorithm, so the proof also computes.

screens.title: A sign change with no root
screens.prose: Let $f(x) = \tfrac1x$ for $x \ne 0$, with $f(0) = 1$, on $[-1, 1]$. A classmate says: $f(-1) = -1 < 0 < 1 = f(1)$, so the theorem gives a root.
screens.question: Where is the root?

options.text: There is none. $f$ is not continuous at 0, so the theorem does not apply.

options.why: You looked where the sign flips. There $f(0) = 1$, not 0.
You trusted the theorem without its hypothesis. On $(-1, 0)$, $\tfrac1x < 0$ throughout.
You blamed the theorem. It holds; its hypothesis, continuity on $[-1, 1]$, fails here.

hints.text: Check every hypothesis before you use a theorem.
Is $f$ continuous at 0?
Near 0, $\tfrac1x$ is unbounded, so no $\delta$ works for $\varepsilon = 1$.

feedback.correct: Right. The sign changes by a jump, not through 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether $f$ is continuous on the whole interval.

byKey.zero: You assumed the sign change happens through 0. $f$ jumps from very negative to very positive, and $f(0) = 1$.

explain.text: $\tfrac1x$ is never 0, and $f(0) = 1$, so there is no root. The theorem needs continuity on all of $[a, b]$, and it fails at 0. Dropping a hypothesis is the most common misuse.

screens.title: The converse fails
screens.prose: A function has the **intermediate value property** if it takes every value between any two of its values. Take $\sin(\tfrac1x)$ with $f(0) = 0$. On every interval $[0, t]$ it swings through all of $[-1, 1]$.
screens.question: Does the intermediate value property imply continuity?

options.text: No: this $f$ has the property, yet l15 showed it is not continuous at 0.
Yes: a function that skips no values cannot jump.
options.why: You reversed the theorem. Continuity implies the property; this $f$ has the property and still breaks continuity at 0.

options.text: The question is empty: $f$ lacks the property near 0.
options.why: You expected a gap. Every value in $[-1, 1]$ is taken in every $[0, t]$, so no value is skipped.
You tried to mend 0. Sequences give limits 1 and $-1$ there, so no value of $f(0)$ makes it continuous.

hints.text: Recall the sequence $x_n = \tfrac{1}{2\pi n + \pi/2}$ from l15.
Along it $f(x_n) = 1 \not\to f(0)$.
So $f$ is not continuous, though it skips no values.

feedback.correct: Right. The theorem is one way only.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Recall whether $\sin(\tfrac1x)$ is continuous at 0.

explain.text: $\sin(\tfrac1x)$ with $f(0) = 0$ takes every value between any two of its values. Yet it is not continuous at 0. So the theorem's converse is false.

screens.title: Bisection as code
screens.prose: Write `bisect(f, a, b, tol)`: halve $[a, b]$, keeping a sign change, until the width is at most `tol`, and return the midpoint. Then `steps_needed(a, b, tol)`: how many halvings that takes. $f(a)$ may be either sign.
screens.question: Complete both functions.

widget.starter:
def bisect(f, a, b, tol):
    """f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs. Halve [a, b] until its
    width is at most tol, keeping a sign change; return the midpoint."""
    ...

def steps_needed(a, b, tol):
    """Number of halvings n until (b - a) / 2**n is at most tol."""
    ...
widget.solution:
def bisect(f, a, b, tol):
    """f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs. Halve [a, b] until its
    width is at most tol, keeping a sign change; return the midpoint."""
    fa = f(a)
    while b - a > tol:
        m = (a + b) / 2
        fm = f(m)
        if fm == 0:
            return m
        if (fm < 0) == (fa < 0):   # same sign as f(a): root is right of m
            a, fa = m, fm
        else:
            b = m
    return (a + b) / 2

def steps_needed(a, b, tol):
    """Number of halvings n until (b - a) / 2**n is at most tol."""
    n, width = 0, b - a
    while width > tol:
        width /= 2
        n += 1
    return n
widget.how: Check runs 13 hidden tests. Six call bisect with lambdas, within 1e-6 or tighter of the root, including one where f(a) > 0 and two that check exactly when the loop stops. Seven check steps_needed exactly, including widths that land exactly on tol.

hints.text: Loop while `b - a > tol`. Compare the sign of $f(m)$ with the sign of $f(a)$.
If $f(m)$ has the sign of $f(a)$, the sign change is in $[m, b]$: move `a` to `m`.
For `steps_needed`, halve the width in a loop and count until it is at most `tol`.

feedback.correct: Right. 20 halvings pin the root of $x^3 - x - 1$ to $10^{-6}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep the half whose ends have opposite signs, and stop as soon as the width is at most `tol`.

explain.text: Each pass keeps the root inside, so the final midpoint is within $\tfrac{\text{tol}}{2}$ of it. Since $2^{19} < 10^6 < 2^{20}$, $[1, 2]$ needs 20 halvings for $10^{-6}$. Comparing signs with $f(a)$ handles either orientation.

screens.title: Implied volatility
screens.prose: A one-year call has spot and strike £100 and zero rates. It costs £3.99 at 10% volatility, £7.97 at 20% and £11.92 at 30%. The price is continuous in volatility. The market quotes £8.
screens.question: The theorem gives an implied volatility in $[0.1, 0.3]$. How many halvings pin it to an interval of width at most 0.0001?

hints.text: The interval $[0.1, 0.3]$ has width 0.2.
After $n$ halvings the width is $\tfrac{0.2}{2^n}$.

feedback.correct: Right. 11 halvings. The implied volatility is about 20.09%.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $\tfrac{0.2}{2^n} \le 0.0001$ for the smallest whole $n$.

byKey.ten: After 10 halvings the width is $\tfrac{0.2}{1024} \approx 0.000195$, still above 0.0001.
byKey.count: You counted steps of 0.0001 across the interval. Halving is far faster: $2^{11} = 2048$.
byKey.from1: You used width 1, as on $[1, 2]$. Here the width is 0.2, so fewer halvings are needed.

explain.text: $\tfrac{0.2}{2^{11}} \approx 0.0000977$, so 11 halvings suffice; the implied volatility is about 0.200867. Continuity is what promises a volatility that fits £8. A price path with an overnight gap is not continuous, so the theorem does not promise every level traded.

ideas: If $f$ is continuous on $[a, b]$ and $f(a) < 0 < f(b)$, some $c \in (a, b)$ has $f(c) = 0$. Applied to $f - y$, $f$ takes every value between $f(a)$ and $f(b)$.
Proof: $c = \sup\{x : f(x) < 0\}$ exists by completeness. $f(c) < 0$ breaks the upper bound, and $f(c) > 0$ gives a smaller one.
Bisection is a second proof and an algorithm. After $n$ halvings the width is $\tfrac{b - a}{2^n}$, so $[1, 2]$ needs 20 for $10^{-6}$.

formula.name: Intermediate value theorem
formula.note: Needs $f$ continuous on $[a, b]$, and gives at least one $c$, not exactly one. The converse fails: $\sin(\tfrac1x)$ with $f(0) = 0$.

summary.trap: Without continuity a sign change proves nothing: $\tfrac1x$ with $f(0) = 1$ changes sign on $[-1, 1]$ and has no root.

options.text: One, by the intermediate value theorem.
options.why: You read the theorem as 'exactly one'. It promises at least one; $x^3 - x = x(x - 1)(x + 1)$ has three.

options.text: None: $g(0) = 0$ is at the middle, not a crossing.
options.why: You discounted a root. $g(0) = 0$ is a root like any other.
